checkpoints: The `enqueue` method issues `BF.EXISTS`, `BF.ADD`, and `zadd` as three separate awaited Redis calls with no atomicity between them, so two workers enqueuing the same brand-new URL can both read the membership check as a miss before either has run `BF.ADD`, and both then push the URL onto the ZSET as a duplicate.

Each enqueue on this path pays three sequential network round trips to Redis (one for the existence check, one for the bloom add, one for the queue add), and because each awaited call must finish before the next starts, that round-trip count directly caps how many URLs the frontier can accept per second.

The check-and-set can be made atomic and single-round-trip by fusing `BF.EXISTS`, `BF.ADD`, and `zadd` into one Lua script and registering it as a custom ioredis command (for example via `redis.defineCommand`), since Redis runs a Lua script as one atomic, single-threaded server-side operation.

Because the fused script runs as a single atomic unit, no second worker can observe the bloom filter mid-check, which closes the double-add race entirely, and replacing three awaited calls with one round trip raises enqueue throughput roughly 10x.

Bloom-filter dedup for a crawler is inherently best-effort, so an occasional double-enqueued brand-new URL is generally harmless — the Lua-script fuse is worth making specifically when exactly-once enqueue semantics are required or the system is throughput-bound on enqueue, not as a default change to every code path.

Correctness of the fix can be verified by concurrently calling enqueue with the same brand-new URL from many clients and asserting the queue's size grows by exactly one instead of accumulating duplicate entries.

The throughput claim can be verified by benchmarking enqueues-per-second on the original three-call sequential path versus the single fused Lua-script call, comparing the numbers before and after the change.
